claim: A key innovation emerging in complex animals is irreversible somatic differentiation where daughters of a vegetative cell perform a vegetative function as well, forming a somatic lineage that can no longer be directly involved in reproduction.
source: A key innovation emerging in complex animals is irreversible somatic differentiation: daughters of a vegetative cell perform a vegetative function as well, thus, forming a somatic lineage that can no longer be directly involved in reproduction.
evidence: This is a definitional statement about irreversible somatic differentiation in complex animals, drawing from established biological knowledge.

claim: Primitive species separate vegetative and reproductive tasks in time rather than in space.
source: Primitive species use a different strategy: vegetative and reproductive tasks are separated in time rather than in space.
evidence: This statement draws from established knowledge about developmental strategies in primitive species.

claim: Three components are necessary for the evolution of irreversible somatic differentiation: costly cell differentiation, vegetative cells that significantly improve organism performance even if present in small numbers, and large enough organism size.
source: Here, we develop an evolutionary model of development of a simple multicellular organism and find that three components are necessary for the evolution of irreversible somatic differentiation: (i) costly cell differentiation, (ii) vegetative cells that significantly improve the organism's performance even if present in small numbers, and (iii) large enough organism size.
evidence: This is the main finding of the study, supported by the computational model and simulations presented throughout the manuscript.

claim: In unicellular species and simple multicellular colonies, reproductive and vegetative functions are performed at different times by the same cells (temporal specialization).
source: In unicellular species and simple multicellular colonies, these two kinds of functions are performed at different times by the same cells – specialization is temporal.
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Mikhailov et al., 2009.

claim: In more complex multicellular organisms, specialization transforms from temporal to spatial, where groups of cells focused on different tasks emerge during organism development.
source: In more complex multicellular organisms, specialization transforms from temporal to spatial (Mikhailov et al., 2009), where groups of cells focused on different tasks emerge in the course of organism development.
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Mikhailov et al., 2009.

claim: The vast majority of metazoans feature irreversible somatic differentiation where any cell performing vegetative functions produces cells performing the same vegetative function.
source: The vast majority of metazoans feature a very specific and extreme pattern of cell differentiation: any cell performing vegetative functions forms a somatic lineage, that is, producing cells performing the same vegetative function – somatic differentiation is irreversible.
evidence: This is a statement about a well-established pattern in metazoan biology.

claim: Somatic cells cannot give rise to reproductive cells and therefore do not have a chance to pass their offspring to the next generation of organisms.
source: Since such somatic cells cannot give rise to reproductive cells, somatic cells do not have a chance to pass their offspring to the next generation of organisms.
evidence: This is a logical consequence of the definition of irreversible somatic differentiation.

claim: The mode of irreversible somatic differentiation opened a way for deeper specialization of somatic cells and consequently to the astonishing complexity of multicellular animals.
source: Such a mode of organism development opened a way for deeper specialization of somatic cells and consequently to the astonishing complexity of multicellular animals.
evidence: This is an inference about the evolutionary consequences of irreversible somatic differentiation.

claim: In Volvocales green algae, the emergence of irreversibly differentiated somatic cells is the hallmark innovation marking the transition from colonial life forms to multicellular species.
source: Outside of the metazoans – in a group of green algae Volvocales serving as a model species for evolution of multicellularity – the emergence of irreversibly differentiated somatic cells is the hallmark innovation marking the transition from colonial life forms to multicellular species (Kirk, 2005).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Kirk, 2005.

claim: The production of individual cells specialized in vegetative functions comes with a number of benefits.
source: While the production of individual cells specialized in vegetative functions comes with a number of benefits (Grosberg and Strathmann, 2007), the development of a dedicated vegetative cell lineage that is lost for organism reproduction is not obviously a beneficial adaptation.
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Grosberg and Strathmann, 2007.

claim: The development of a dedicated vegetative cell lineage that is lost for organism reproduction is not obviously a beneficial adaptation.
source: While the production of individual cells specialized in vegetative functions comes with a number of benefits (Grosberg and Strathmann, 2007), the development of a dedicated vegetative cell lineage that is lost for organism reproduction is not obviously a beneficial adaptation.
evidence: This is a reasoning statement that motivates the research question.

claim: Exceptions from irreversible somatic differentiation are widespread in plants.
source: For example, exceptions from irreversible somatic differentiation are widespread in plants (Lanfear, 2018) and are even known in simpler metazoans among cnidarians (DuBuc et al., 2020) for which differentiation from vegetative to reproductive functions has been reported.
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Lanfear, 2018.

claim: Exceptions from irreversible somatic differentiation are known in simpler metazoans among cnidarians, for which differentiation from vegetative to reproductive functions has been reported.
source: For example, exceptions from irreversible somatic differentiation are widespread in plants (Lanfear, 2018) and are even known in simpler metazoans among cnidarians (DuBuc et al., 2020) for which differentiation from vegetative to reproductive functions has been reported.
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to DuBuc et al., 2020.

claim: The irreversibility of somatic differentiation cannot be taken for granted in the course of the evolution of complex multicellularity.
source: Therefore, the irreversibility of somatic differentiation cannot be taken for granted in the course of the evolution of complex multicellularity.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the existence of exceptions to irreversible somatic differentiation.

claim: Terminally differentiated cells lose the ability to divide, unlike irreversibly differentiated cells who are capable of cell division.
source: Terminal differentiation is a type of cell differentiation different from irreversible cell differentiation. Unlike irreversibly differentiated cells who are capable of cell division, terminally differentiated cells lose the ability to divide.
evidence: This is a definitional distinction between two types of cell differentiation.

claim: Heterocysts of cyanobacteria perform nitrogen fixation, which requires anaerobic conditions, and therefore these cells are very limited in resources and do not divide.
source: For example heterocysts of cyanobacteria perform nitrogen fixation, which requires anaerobic conditions, therefore these cells are very limited in resources and do not divide.
evidence: This is an example of terminal differentiation based on established biological knowledge.

claim: The majority of theoretical models addressing the evolution of somatic cells focuses on the evolution of cell specialization, abstracting from the developmental process of how germ and soma are produced during organism growth.
source: The majority of the theoretical models addressing the evolution of somatic cells focuses on the evolution of cell specialization, abstracting from the developmental process how germ (reproductive specialists) and soma are produced in the course of the organism growth.
evidence: This is a characterization of the existing literature, supported by multiple citations in the following sentences.

claim: A large amount of work focuses on the optimal distribution of reproductive and vegetative functions in the adult organism.
source: For example, a large amount of work focuses on the optimal distribution of reproductive and vegetative functions in the adult organism (Michod, 2007; Willensdorfer, 2009; Rossetti et al., 2010; Rueffler et al., 2012; Ispolatov et al., 2012; Goldsby et al., 2012; Solari et al., 2013; Goldsby et al., 2014; Amado et al., 2018; Tverskoi et al., 2018).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations.

claim: In Gavrilets, 2010, the organism development is considered, but the fraction of cells capable of becoming somatic is fixed and does not evolve.
source: In Gavrilets, 2010, the organism development is considered, but the fraction of cells capable of becoming somatic is fixed and does not evolve.
evidence: This is a characterization of a specific study.

claim: In Erten and Kokko, 2020, the strategy of germ-to-soma differentiation is an evolvable trait, but the irreversibility of somatic differentiation is taken for granted.
source: In Erten and Kokko, 2020, the strategy of germ-to-soma differentiation is an evolvable trait, but the irreversibility of somatic differentiation is taken for granted.
evidence: This is a characterization of a specific study.

claim: In Rodrigues et al., 2012, irreversible differentiation was found, but both considered cell types pass to the next generation of organisms, such that the irreversible specialists are not truly somatic cells in the sense of evolutionary dead ends.
source: In Rodrigues et al., 2012, irreversible differentiation was found, but both considered cell types pass to the next generation of organisms, such that the irreversible specialists are not truly somatic cells in the sense of evolutionary dead ends.
evidence: This is a characterization of a specific study.

claim: In Cooper and West, 2018, a broad scope of cell differentiation patterns has been investigated in the context of evolution of cooperation, but irreversible somatic differentiation was not considered.
source: Finally, in Cooper and West, 2018 a broad scope of cell differentiation patterns has been investigated in the context of evolution of cooperation. However, irreversible somatic differentiation was not considered in the study.
evidence: This is a characterization of a specific study.

claim: The theoretical understanding of the evolution of irreversibly differentiated somatic cell lines is limited so far.
source: Hence, the theoretical understanding of the evolution of irreversibly differentiated somatic cell lines is limited so far.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the review of existing literature.

claim: The model considers a large population of clonally developing organisms composed of two types of cells: germ-role and soma-role.
source: We consider a large population of clonally developing organisms composed of two types of cells: germ-role and soma-role.
evidence: This is a description of the model setup.

claim: Soma-role cells die at the end of the organism life cycle, while germ-role cells continue to live.
source: The roles differ in the ability to survive beyond the end of the organism life cycle: soma-role cells die at the end, while germ-role cells continue to live.
evidence: This is a description of the model setup.

claim: Each organism is initiated as a single germ-role cell.
source: Each organism is initiated as a single germ-role cell.
evidence: This is a description of the model setup.

claim: Immediately upon reaching maturity, the organism reproduces: germ-role cells disperse and each becomes a newborn organism, while all soma-role cells die.
source: Immediately upon reaching maturity, the organism reproduces: germ-role cells disperse and each becomes a newborn organism, while all soma-role cells die and are thus lost, see Figure 1A.
evidence: This is a description of the model setup, with reference to Figure 1A.

claim: Soma-role cells are capable to accelerate growth: an organism containing more somatic cells grows faster.
source: We assume that soma-role cells are capable to accelerate growth: an organism containing more somatic cells grows faster, so having soma-role cells during the life cycle is beneficial for the organism.
evidence: This is an assumption of the model.

claim: The life cycle of an organism starts with a single germ-role cell, and when the organism reaches maturity, each germ-role cell becomes a newborn organism and each soma-role cell dies.
source: The life cycle of an organism starts with a single germ-role cell. In each round, all cells divide and daughter cells can differentiate into a role different from the maternal cell's role. When the organism reaches maturity, it reproduces: each germ-role cell becomes a newborn organism and each soma-role cell dies.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1A and described in the text.

claim: Change of cell roles is controlled by a stochastic developmental strategy defined by probabilities of each possible outcome of a cell division.
source: Change of cell roles is controlled by a stochastic developmental strategy defined by probabilities of each possible outcomes of a cell division.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1B and described in the text.

claim: When a cell divides, the two daughter cells can change their role, leading to three possible combinations: two germ-role cells, one germ-role cell plus one soma-role cell, or two soma-role cells.
source: When a cell divides, the two daughter cells can change their role, leading to three possible combinations: two germ-role cells, one germ-role cell plus one soma-role cell, or two soma-role cells.
evidence: This is a description of the model setup.

claim: Evolution of the developmental strategy is driven by the growth competition between populations executing different strategies.
source: In our model, evolution of the developmental strategy is driven by the growth competition between populations executing different strategies – these populations able to produce more offspring and/or complete their life cycle faster gain a selective advantage.
evidence: This is a description of the model approach.

claim: Fitness in the growth competition is measured by the population growth rate in a stationary regime of exponential growth.
source: Specifically, we measure the fitness in the growth competition by the population growth rate in a stationary regime of exponential growth (Pichugin et al., 2017; Gao et al., 2019).
evidence: This is a description of the model approach, supported by citations.

claim: The rate of population growth is determined by the number of offspring produced by an organism and the time needed for an organism to develop from a single cell to maturity.
source: The rate of population growth is determined by the number of offspring produced by an organism (equal to the number of germ-role cells at the end of life cycle) and the time needed for an organism to develop from a single cell to maturity (improved with the number of soma-role cells during the life cycle).
evidence: This is a description of the model approach.

claim: Resource distribution among cells is coordinated at the level of the organism such that cell division is synchronous.
source: Here, we assume that resource distribution among cells is coordinated at the level of the organism: Cells which need more resources will get more, such that cell division is synchronous.
evidence: This is an assumption of the model.

claim: The differentiation of a cell requires efforts to modify epigenetic marks in the genome, recalibration of regulatory networks, synthesis of additional and utilization of no longer necessary proteins.
source: The differentiation of a cell requires efforts to modify epigenetic marks in the genome, recalibration of regulatory networks, synthesis of additional and utilization of no longer necessary proteins.
evidence: This is a biological justification for the model assumption, based on general knowledge.

claim: Soma-role cells can benefit to the organism growth only if their proportion in the organism exceeds the contribution threshold x0.
source: With the functional form (3), soma-role cells can benefit to the organism growth, only if their proportion in the organism exceeds the contribution threshold x0.
evidence: This is a description of the model parameter.

claim: Previous works have shown that convex (accelerating) performance functions favour cell differentiation.
source: Previous works have shown that convex (accelerating) performance functions favour cell differentiation (Michod, 2006; Rueffler et al., 2012; Cooper and West, 2018).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations.

claim: The form of functions favoring cell differentiation has been extended to be concave (decelerating) by including topological constraints in organisms.
source: Lately, the form of functions favoring cell differentiation has been extended to be concave (decelerating) by including topological constraints in organisms (Yanni et al., 2020).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Yanni et al., 2020.

claim: When somatic differentiation is irreversible, the fraction of germ-role cells can only decrease in the course of life cycle.
source: This finding comes from the fact that when somatic differentiation is irreversible, the fraction of germ-role cells can only decrease in the course of life cycle.
evidence: This is a logical consequence of the definition of irreversible differentiation.

claim: Irreversible strategies deal with the tradeoff between producing more soma-role cells at the beginning of the life cycle and having more germ-role cells by the end of it.
source: As a result, irreversible strategies deal with the tradeoff between producing more soma-role cells at the beginning of the life cycle, and having more germ-role cells by the end of it.
evidence: This is an inference about the constraints on irreversible strategies.

claim: Reversible somatic differentiation strategies do not experience a similar tradeoff as irreversible strategies, as germ-role cells can be generated from soma-role cells.
source: By contrast, reversible somatic differentiation strategies do not experience a similar tradeoff, as germ-role cells can be generated from soma-role cells.
evidence: This is an inference about the advantages of reversible strategies.

claim: Reversible strategy allows higher differentiation rates and can develop a high soma-role cell fraction during organism growth and at the same time have a large number of germ-role cells by the moment of reproduction.
source: As a result, reversible strategy allows higher differentiation rates and can develop a high soma-role cell fraction in the course of the organism growth and at the same time have a large number of germ-role cells by the moment of reproduction.
evidence: This is an inference about the advantages of reversible strategies.

claim: Under costless cell differentiation, for any irreversible strategy, we can find a reversible differentiation counterpart which leads to faster growth.
source: Under costless cell differentiation, for any irreversible strategy, we can find a reversible differentiation counterpart, which leads to faster growth: the development proceeds faster, while the expected number of produced offspring is the same, see Appendix 2 for details.
evidence: This is a finding from the model analysis, with details in Appendix 2.

claim: Costless cell differentiation cannot lead to irreversible somatic differentiation.
source: As a result, costless cell differentiation cannot lead to irreversible somatic differentiation.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the model results.

claim: Evolutionarily optimal reversible strategies feature much larger rates of cell differentiation than evolutionarily optimal irreversible strategies.
source: We found that evolutionarily optimal reversible strategies feature much larger rates of cell differentiation than evolutionarily optimal irreversible strategies, see Figure 2D.
evidence: This is a finding from the model simulations, shown in Figure 2D.

claim: Even at large costs where frequent differentiation is heavily penalized, the distinction between differentiation rates of reversible and irreversible strategies remains apparent.
source: Even at large costs, where frequent differentiation is heavily penalized, the distinction between differentiation rates of reversible and irreversible strategies remains apparent.
evidence: This is a finding from the model simulations.

claim: Irreversible strategies are insensitive to high soma-to-germ costs, since soma-role cells never differentiate.
source: Irreversible strategies are insensitive to high soma-to-germ costs, since soma-role cells never differentiate.
evidence: This is an inference about the properties of irreversible strategies.

claim: Reversible strategies are heavily punished by high costs of soma-role differentiation.
source: At the same time, reversible strategies are heavily punished by high costs of soma-role differentiation.
evidence: This is an inference about the properties of reversible strategies.

claim: Irreversible strategies are consistently observed in regions of the costs space where the asymmetry is opposite (it is hard to go from germ to soma but easy to return back).
source: However, irreversible strategies are consistently observed in other regions of the costs space, even including these, where the asymmetry is opposite (it is hard to go from germ to soma but easy to return back), see Figure 2A,H.
evidence: This is a finding from the model simulations, shown in Figure 2A,H.

claim: Irreversible strategies are only able to evolve when the soma-role cells contribute to the organism cell doubling time even if present in small proportions.
source: We found that irreversible strategies are only able to evolve when the soma-role cells contribute to the organism cell doubling time even if present in small proportions, see Figure 3A,B.
evidence: This is a finding from the model simulations, shown in Figure 3A,B.

claim: The contribution threshold value (x0) has to be small for irreversible differentiation to be promoted.
source: First, the contribution threshold value (x0) has to be small, see Figure 3D – irreversible differentiation is promoted when soma-role cells begin to contribute to the organism growth even in low numbers.
evidence: This is a finding from the model simulations, shown in Figure 3D.

claim: The most crucial factor promoting irreversible somatic differentiation is the effectiveness of soma-role cells at small numbers.
source: Together, these patterns give an evidence that the most crucial factor promoting irreversible somatic differentiation is the effectiveness of soma-role cells at small numbers, see Appendix 4 for more detailed data presentation.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the model results.

claim: The optimal germ-to-soma differentiation rate is found as a balance between the needs to deploy soma-role cells early on and to keep the high number of germ-role by the end of the life cycle.
source: Therefore, the optimal germ-to-soma differentiation rate is found as a balance between the needs to deploy soma-role cells early on and to keep the high number of germ-role by the end of the life cycle.
evidence: This is an inference about the optimization of differentiation strategies.

claim: Irreversible somatic differentiation strategies produce soma-role cells at lower rate than reversible strategies.
source: This implies that irreversible somatic differentiation strategies produce soma-role cells at lower rate than reversible strategies, see Figure 2D.
evidence: This is a finding from the model simulations, shown in Figure 2D.

claim: With irreversible differentiation, an organism spends a significant amount of time having only a few soma-role cells.
source: With irreversible differentiation, an organism spends a significant amount of time having only a few soma-role cells.
evidence: This is an inference about the dynamics of irreversible strategies.

claim: The irreversible strategy can only be evolutionarily successful if the few soma-role cells have a notable contribution to the organism growth time.
source: Hence, the irreversible strategy can only be evolutionarily successful, if the few soma-role cells have a notable contribution to the organism growth time.
evidence: This is an inference about the conditions for success of irreversible strategies.

claim: When the maximal benefit is too small, the cell differentiation just does not provide enough benefits to be selected for and the evolutionarily optimal strategy is no differentiation.
source: When the maximal benefit is too small, the cell differentiation just does not provide enough benefits to be selected for and the evolutionarily optimal strategy is no differentiation.
evidence: This is an inference about the model results.

claim: When the maximal benefit is very close to one, the cell doubling time approaches zero, and the benefits of having many soma-role cells outweighs the costs of differentiation and the optimal strategy is reversible.
source: In the opposite case, when the maximal benefit is very close to one, the cell doubling time approaches zero, see Equation (3). Then, the benefits of having many soma-role cells outweighs the costs of differentiation and the optimal strategy is reversible, see Appendix 4.
evidence: This is an inference about the model results.

claim: Either reversible strategies or the no differentiation strategy evolve in small organisms.
source: We found that either reversible strategies or the no differentiation strategy evolve in small organisms.
evidence: This is a finding from the model simulations.

claim: Reversible strategies can quickly reach a fixed fraction of soma-role cells, thus they can obtain maximised benefits from soma-role cells with small maturity sizes.
source: Since reversible strategies can quickly reach a fixed fraction of soma-role cells, thus they can obtain maximised benefits from soma-role cells with small maturity sizes (Appendix 2—figure 1).
evidence: This is an inference about the properties of reversible strategies.

claim: The no differentiation strategy does not involve cell differentiation, so they do not have cell differentiation costs.
source: Since the no differentiation strategy does not involve cell differentiation, they do not have cell differentiation costs.
evidence: This is a logical consequence of the definition of no differentiation strategy.

claim: Irreversible strategies increase the fraction of soma-roles and increase the benefits of soma-role cells gradually as maturity size increases.
source: In contrast, irreversible strategies increase the fraction of soma-roles and increase the benefits of soma-role cells gradually as maturity size increases.
evidence: This is an inference about the properties of irreversible strategies.

claim: The cell differentiation costs for irreversible strategies decrease as maturity size increases as the fraction of germ-role cells decreases.
source: Meanwhile, the cell differentiation costs for irreversible strategies decrease as maturity size increases as the fraction of germ-role cells decreases.
evidence: This is an inference about the properties of irreversible strategies.

claim: Compared with other strategies, the irreversible strategies have advantages in large organisms.
source: Thus compared with other strategies, the irreversible strategies have advantages in large organisms.
evidence: This is an inference about the properties of irreversible strategies.

claim: Organisms performing just a few more rounds of cell divisions than 64 cells are able to evolve irreversible differentiation at a wide range of cell differentiation costs.
source: At the same time, organisms performing just a few more rounds of cell divisions are able to evolve irreversible differentiation at a wide range of cell differentiation costs, see also Appendix 5.
evidence: This is a finding from the model simulations.

claim: The evolution of irreversible somatic differentiation is strongly tied to the size of the organism.
source: This indicates that the evolution of irreversible somatic differentiation is strongly tied to the size of the organism.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the model results.

claim: Irreversible strategies were found in a narrow range of cell differentiation costs at maturity size 32 cells and the fraction of composition effect profiles that allow evolution of irreversible differentiation there was quite low – about 1%.
source: However, irreversible strategies were found in a narrow range of cell differentiation costs and the fraction of composition effect profiles that allow evolution of irreversible differentiation there was quite low – about 1%.
evidence: This is a finding from the model simulations.

claim: For irreversible somatic differentiation to evolve, the organism size should exceed a threshold of roughly 64 cells.
source: Hence, for irreversible somatic differentiation to evolve, the organism size should exceed a threshold of roughly 64 cells.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the model results.

claim: The process of cell differentiation may impact the organism development by posing a risk of dysregulation resulting in an emergence of selfish mutants that could cause cancer.
source: However, the process of cell differentiation may impact the organism development in another way. Differentiation requires modifications in DNA regulation, which in turn poses a risk of dysregulation resulting in an emergence of selfish mutants that could for example cause cancer.
evidence: This is a biological reasoning based on general knowledge.

claim: The disposable soma theory suggests that cells performing vegetative functions form separate lineages to contain emerging mutations and prevent them from passing to the next generations of organisms.
source: The disposable soma theory suggests that cells performing vegetative functions form separate lineages to contain emerging mutations and prevent them from passing to the next generations of organisms.
evidence: This is a reference to an established theory in biology.

claim: The results obtained with a model of risky differentiation are very similar to the outcomes of the main model where cell differentiation causes delay.
source: The results obtained with a model of risky differentiation are very similar to the outcomes of our main model, where cell differentiation cause delay, see Figure 5.
evidence: This is a finding from the alternative model, shown in Figure 5.

claim: In both models (delay and risk), irreversible differentiation only evolves if cell differentiation does not come for free but brings costly side-effects.
source: In both models, irreversible differentiation only evolves if cell differentiation does not come for free but brings costly side-effects (delay or risk).
evidence: This is a comparison of findings from two model variants.

claim: In both models (delay and risk), irreversible differentiation is prevalent when costs of soma-to-germ transitions are intense; reversible differentiation is prevalent when costs of both transitions are low; and no differentiation is prevalent when costs of germ-to-soma transitions are intense.
source: Also, in both models irreversible differentiation is prevalent when costs of soma-to-germ transitions are intense; reversible differentiation is prevalent when costs of both transitions are low; and no differentiation is prevalent when costs of germ-to-soma transitions are intense Figure 2A–C.
evidence: This is a comparison of findings from two model variants, shown in Figure 2A–C.

claim: Cell differentiation costs are essential for the emergence of irreversible somatic differentiation.
source: According to our results, cell differentiation costs are essential for the emergence of irreversible somatic differentiation, see Figure 2A.
evidence: This is a key finding of the study, shown in Figure 2A.

claim: The costs punish strategies with high rate of cell differentiation, and as a result, irreversible strategies gain an advantage because their overall differentiation rate is low.
source: The costs punish strategies with high rate of cell differentiation. As a result, irreversible strategies gain an advantage because their overall differentiation rate is low, see Figure 2D, and soma-role cells do not differentiate at all.
evidence: This is an explanation of the mechanism behind the key finding, shown in Figure 2D.

claim: Most models focus on traits that lead to benefits for the organism, while the cost of cell differentiation are rarely considered.
source: Most models focus on traits that lead to benefits for the organism, while the cost of cell differentiation are rarely considered.
evidence: This is a characterization of the existing literature.

claim: For cells in a multicellular organism, differentiation costs arise from the material needs, energy, and time it takes to produce components necessary for the performance of the differentiated cell, which were absent in the parent cell.
source: For cells in a multicellular organism, differentiation costs arise from the material needs, energy, and time it takes to produce components necessary for the performance of the differentiated cell, which were absent in the parent cell.
evidence: This is a biological explanation based on general knowledge.

claim: In filamentous cyanobacteria nitrogen-fixating heterocysts develop much thicker cell wall than parent photosynthetic cells had.
source: For instance, in filamentous cyanobacteria nitrogen-fixating heterocysts develop much thicker cell wall than parent photosynthetic cells had.
evidence: This is an example from biology based on established knowledge.

claim: Reports indicate between 23% and 74% of the proteome changes its abundance in heterocysts compared against photosynthetic cells.
source: Also, reports indicate between 23% (Ow et al., 2008) and 74% (Sandh et al., 2014) of the proteome changes its abundance in heterocysts compared against photosynthetic cells.
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Ow et al., 2008 and Sandh et al., 2014.

claim: Changes in the protein composition in the course of cell differentiation was found during the development of stalk and fruiting bodies of Dictyostelium discoideum.
source: Similarly, the changes in the protein composition in the course of cell differentiation was found during the development of stalk and fruiting bodies of Dictyostelium discoideum (Bakthavatsalam and Gomer, 2010; Czarna et al., 2010).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Bakthavatsalam and Gomer, 2010 and Czarna et al., 2010.

claim: The exact mechanism of the differentiation costs does not play a major role in the evolution of irreversible somatic differentiation.
source: These results indicate that the exact mechanism of the differentiation costs does not play a major role in the evolution of irreversible somatic differentiation.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from comparing the delay and risk models.

claim: Irreversible somatic differentiation is more likely to evolve when a few soma-role cells are able to provide a substantial benefit to the organism.
source: Our model demonstrates that irreversible somatic differentiation is more likely to evolve when a few soma-role cells are able to provide a substantial benefit to the organism, see Figure 3.
evidence: This is a key finding of the study, shown in Figure 3.

claim: In Eudorina illinoiensis, only four out of thirty-two cells are vegetative.
source: In Eudorina illinoiensis, only four out of thirty-two cells are vegetative (Sambamurty AVSS, 2005) (soma-role in our terms).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Sambamurty AVSS, 2005.

claim: It seems possible that highly-efficient soma-role cells open the way to the evolution of irreversible somatic differentiation.
source: Thus, it seems possible that highly-efficient soma-role cells open the way to the evolution of irreversible somatic differentiation.
evidence: This is a speculation based on the model results and biological examples.

claim: Several patterns of how cells proved the benefit to an organism have been previously considered.
source: Several patterns of how cells proved the benefit to an organism have been previously considered (Michod, 2007; Willensdorfer, 2009; Rossetti et al., 2010; Rueffler et al., 2012; Cooper and West, 2018; Yanni et al., 2020).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations.

claim: The majority of papers focuses on the resource allocation toward different tasks in each cell in an organism and how divergent different cells can be.
source: The majority of papers focuses on the resource allocation toward different tasks in each cell in an organism and how divergent different cells can be.
evidence: This is a characterization of the existing literature.

claim: In the model, the authors assume that the germ-role and soma-role cell are different in function and focus on the relationship between the number of soma-role cells and their impact.
source: In our model, we assume that the germ-role and soma-role cell are different in function and focus on the relationship between the number of soma-role cells and their impact, e.g. the character of their interactions.
evidence: This is a description of the model approach.

claim: Irreversible somatic differentiation does not evolve if the organism size is small.
source: Our model shows that irreversible somatic differentiation does not evolve if the organism size is small, see Figure 4A.
evidence: This is a key finding of the study, shown in Figure 4A.

claim: The maturity size plays an important role in an organism's life cycle.
source: The maturity size plays an important role in an organism's life cycle (Amado et al., 2018; Erten and Kokko, 2020):
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Amado et al., 2018 and Erten and Kokko, 2020.

claim: Large organisms have potential advantages to optimize themselves in multiple ways, such as to improve growth efficiency, to avoid predators, to increase problem-solving efficiency, and to exploit the division of labour in organisms.
source: Large organisms have potential advantages to optimize themselves in multiple ways, such as to improve growth efficiency (Waters et al., 2010), to avoid predators (Matz and Kjelleberg, 2005; Fisher et al., 2016; Hiltunen and Becks, 2014), to increase problem-solving efficiency (Morand-Ferron and Quinn, 2011), and to exploit the division of labour in organisms (Carroll, 2001; Matt and Umen, 2016).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations.

claim: The maximum size has been related to the reproduction of the organism from the onset of multicellularity in Earth's history.
source: Moreover, the maximum size has been related to the reproduction of the organism from the onset of multicellularity in Earth's history (Ratcliff et al., 2012).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Ratcliff et al., 2012.

For example, a maternal organism can provide protection and nurture for offspring at their early stages of growth, like in V. carteri (10,000 cells) in which offspring colonies develop inside the parental organism.
